recipes.verso: Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda… con sus huevos rancheros.
recipes.name: Huevos Rancheros
recipes.en: Ranch-style fried eggs in salsa ranchera
recipes.story: The almuerzo of the rancho: fried eggs on soft fried tortillas, covered with a cooked salsa of charred tomato and chile. The salsa is served warm, not raw like pico de gallo, and the beans go on the side.

ingredients.title: Salsa ranchera
items: ¼ white onion, plus 2 thin slices of onion

ingredients.title: Los huevos
items: 3–4 tbsp lard or oil, for the tortillas and eggs

steps: Char the tomatoes, chiles, onion chunk and garlic on a dry comal, turning, until blistered and soft: about 8 minutes for the garlic and chiles, 12 for the tomatoes. Peel the garlic.
Blend or grind them in the molcajete with a pinch of salt. Keep it a little chunky.
Heat the lard in a small pan and fry the onion slices until soft. Pour in the salsa (it will sizzle) and simmer 5–8 minutes, until it darkens and thickens slightly. Season and keep warm.
In a skillet, heat a thin layer of lard. Fry each tortilla about 10 seconds per side, so it softens and puffs a little but doesn't turn into a tostada. Drain and set two on each plate.
In the same skillet, fry the eggs over medium-high, spooning hot fat over the whites until they set with lacy, crisp edges and the yolks stay runny. Salt them.
Set an egg on each tortilla and spoon the hot salsa over the whites, leaving the yolks showing.
Serve right away with refritos, queso fresco, avocado and cilantro.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Huevos rancheros are done in 25 minutes at the comal and skillet. If you want refritos on the side, the beans can come from the pressure cooker (see Frijoles de la Olla).
tips: Fry the tortillas soft, not crisp. You should be able to cut them with the side of your fork.
Make a double batch of salsa ranchera. It keeps 4 days in the fridge and saves the next breakfast.
Lard for the eggs gives the crisp edges abuela's had.

variations.name: Huevos Divorciados
variations.note: The divorced eggs: one in red salsa, one in green, kept apart by a line of refried beans. Diner breakfast all over Mexico.

items: 4 fried tortillas and 4 fried eggs, as in the base
1 cup salsa verde cocida (see Salsa Roja de Molcajete, Variantes)
Queso fresco and chilaquiles or totopos on the side, optional

steps: For each plate, set two tortillas side by side and put an egg on each.
Cover one with red salsa and the other with green.
Spoon a line of refried beans between them to keep them apart.
Top with queso fresco.

variations.name: Huevos Motuleños
variations.en: Yucatecan stacked eggs with ham and plantain
variations.note: From the town of Motul: a crisp tortilla spread with black beans, a fried egg, tomato sauce, ham and peas, with fried plantain on the side. Usually credited to Jorge Siqueff at La Sin Rival in Motul, around 1921.

items: 1 cup salsa ranchera made with habanero instead of serrano (or plain tomato sauce)

steps: Warm the salsa with the ham and peas for 3 minutes.
Spread each crisp tortilla with black beans and top with a fried egg.
Spoon the salsa with ham and peas over the eggs and sprinkle with queso.
Serve with the fried plantain.

recipes.verso: Bolillo, frijol y queso: el desayuno del recreo.
recipes.name: Molletes
recipes.story: Bolillos split open, toasted with butter, spread with refried beans and broiled under melted cheese, then topped with cold pico de gallo. The breakfast of cafés and school mornings in the capital, and the best use for yesterday's bread.

ingredients.title: Molletes
items: 4 bolillos (day-old is fine), or crusty French rolls
2 cups frijoles refritos, warm and thick
2 cups shredded melting cheese: queso Chihuahua, manchego mexicano or Oaxaca

steps: Heat the broiler (or the oven to 425°F). Mix all the pico de gallo ingredients and let stand while you make the molletes.
Split the bolillos lengthwise. Pull out a little of the soft crumb so the beans have room.
Butter the cut sides and toast them, cut side up, 2–3 minutes until the edges are golden.
Spread each half generously with refritos, edge to edge so the bread doesn't burn.
Cover with cheese and broil 2–4 minutes, until melted and bubbling in spots.
Top with pico de gallo and serve with salsa on the side.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version for the molletes themselves, but the beans can come from the pressure cooker (see Frijoles de la Olla, then Frijoles Refritos).
tips: The refritos should be thick enough to hold a line. Runny beans make soggy bread.
Butter first, then toast, then beans. That way the bread stays crisp underneath.

variations.name: Molletes con Chorizo
variations.note: The most common add-on at fondas.
steps: Fry the chorizo, breaking it up, until crisp. Drain off most of the fat (or fry the beans in it).
Spread the beans on the toasted bread, scatter chorizo over them, add the cheese and broil.
Top with pico de gallo.

variations.name: Molletes Dulces
variations.note: The sweet version kids ask for, with a cup of café con leche or champurrado.

items: ¼ cup sugar mixed with 1 tsp ground canela

steps: Butter the cut sides generously.
Sprinkle with the cinnamon sugar.
Broil 2–3 minutes, until the sugar melts and bubbles. Watch closely; it burns fast.

recipes.verso: Verde, blanco y colorado: la bandera en el plato.
recipes.name: Huevos a la Mexicana
recipes.en: Eggs scrambled with tomato, onion and chile
recipes.story: Red tomato, white onion and green chile, the colors of the flag, scrambled with eggs. It's the breakfast every Mexican home makes without a recipe, and it's what goes into a taco on the way out the door.

ingredients.title: Huevos
items: 1–2 serranos, finely chopped (seeds in for more heat)

ingredients.title: Para servir
items: Frijoles de la olla or refritos

steps: Heat the lard in a skillet over medium. Add the onion and serrano and cook 2 minutes, until soft but not browned.
Add the tomato and a pinch of salt. Cook 2–3 minutes, until it softens and most of its juice cooks off.
Beat the eggs lightly with a pinch of salt and pour them into the pan.
Stir gently with a spatula over medium-low until just set, still soft and moist.
Add the cilantro if using and serve right away with beans, tortillas and salsa.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. It's a 10-minute skillet breakfast.
tips: Let the tomato cook down first, or the eggs turn watery.
Some abuelas don't beat the eggs first: they crack them right into the pan and stir, so you get streaks of white and yolk.
Leftovers make the best tacos de huevo for lunch.

variations.name: Huevos con Chorizo
variations.note: The other everyday breakfast taco. Some families add a diced potato fried with the chorizo.
steps: Fry the chorizo in a dry skillet, breaking it up, until it releases its red fat, about 4 minutes. Add the onion and potato and cook until the potato is tender, about 8 minutes.
Pour off extra fat if there's a lot. Add the eggs and stir until just set.
Taste before salting; chorizo is salty.

variations.name: Huevos con Nopales
variations.note: A Lent favorite, and a way to stretch the eggs.

items: 1 cup cooked nopales, in strips (from a jar, rinsed, or fresh and boiled)

steps: Make the base through step 2, adding the nopales with the tomato and cooking until any slime has cooked off.
Add the eggs and stir until just set.

recipes.verso: Carne seca y huevo revuelto, en tortilla de harina envuelto.
recipes.name: Machaca con Huevo
recipes.en: Dried shredded beef scrambled with eggs
recipes.story: Machaca is beef that was salted, sun-dried and pounded so it would keep for months on the ranches of the north. A small handful fried with onion, tomato and chile and scrambled with eggs makes a breakfast wrapped in flour tortillas, the tortilla of the north.

ingredients.title: Machaca
items: 1 cup (about 2 oz) machaca (dried shredded beef, sold in bags at Mexican markets, or see Machaca Casera)
1–2 jalapeños or serranos, chopped, or 1 roasted chile verde (Anaheim), in strips, the Sonora way

ingredients.title: Para servir
items: Frijoles de la olla or refritos

steps: If your machaca is in big strands, pull it apart with your fingers. Taste a piece. If it's very salty or hard, soak it in warm water 5 minutes and squeeze it dry.
Heat the lard in a skillet over medium. Fry the machaca 1–2 minutes, stirring, until it smells toasty and crisps a little.
Add the onion and chile and cook 3 minutes until soft. Add the tomato and cook 2 minutes more.
Beat the eggs lightly without salt; the machaca is already salty.
Pour the eggs into the pan and stir gently over medium-low until just set, still soft and moist.
Taste, add salt only if needed, and serve right away with flour tortillas, beans and salsa.
recipes.pressureNote: The eggs are a quick skillet job, but you can make the machaca itself in the pressure cooker. See Machaca Casera under Variantes.
tips: Go easy on the salt. Taste the machaca first; most of it is salted.
In Monterrey they call this machacado con huevo and make it with more tomato and chile, almost saucy. Nuevo León traces it to Ciénega de Flores, where la Tía Lencha fed it to road crews in the 1920s.
Leftover machaca keeps for weeks in a jar in the fridge.

variations.name: Machaca Casera
variations.note: Real sun-dried machaca is hard to find outside the north. This oven-dried version gets close.

items: 2 lb beef flank or skirt steak, in 3 pieces
1 tbsp salt, plus more to taste

steps: Simmer the beef with the onion, garlic, salt and water to cover 2 hours, until it shreds easily.
Drain and shred it very finely with two forks or your fingers.
Toss with the lime juice, pepper and a little more salt.
Spread thinly on sheet pans and dry in a 200°F oven 2–3 hours, stirring every 30 minutes, until dry and leathery but not burnt.
Pound it in a molcajete or pulse briefly in a food processor until it's fluffy and fine. Store in a jar in the fridge.
variations.pressureNote: Cook the beef with the onion, garlic, salt and 2 cups water at high pressure 35 minutes, natural release 15. Then shred, season and oven-dry as above.

variations.name: Burritos de Machaca
variations.note: In Sonora and Ciudad Juárez burritos are slim and simple, just a filling and a thin flour tortilla. No rice inside.

items: Machaca con huevo from the base
Large thin flour tortillas (sobaqueras if you can find them)

steps: Warm the tortillas on the comal until soft and spotted.
Spread a thin line of beans if using, add a line of machaca con huevo, and roll tightly.
Set seam side down on the comal 30 seconds to seal. Eat with salsa.

recipes.verso: Crujientes o aguaditos, pero siempre bien bañaditos.
recipes.name: Chilaquiles Verdes
recipes.en: Tortilla chips simmered in green salsa
recipes.story: Breakfast made from whatever tortillas are in the kitchen: fried, tossed in salsa or chile, and covered with crema and cheese, or cooked together with eggs. The name comes from the Nahuatl chīlāquilitl, roughly 'soaked in chile'. ¿Crujientes o aguados? ¿Frijoles encima o al lado? Every house decides.

ingredients.title: Totopos
items: 12 corn tortillas, cut in 6 wedges: day-old is the classic, but store-bought or same-morning work fine

steps: Cut the tortillas. Store-bought tortillas fry fine as they are. Very fresh, moist homemade ones splatter less if they sit out on the counter a few minutes first.
Fry in hot oil in batches until golden. For crunchy chilaquiles fry them crisp; for soft ones, take them out while they're still a little chewy. Drain and salt.
Simmer the tomatillos and serranos 8 minutes. Blend with the onion, garlic, cilantro and broth.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and fry the salsa 5 minutes with the epazote.
Add the totopos and toss: 1 minute for crunchy, 3 for soft.
Serve right away with crema, queso, onion, avocado and an egg or chicken, with beans on the side.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Chilaquiles take 30 minutes and have to be eaten the moment they're ready.
tips: Drain the fried tortillas well. Fresher tortillas hold a little more oil.
Leftover red chile from enchiladas or tamales makes great chilaquiles.

variations.name: Chilaquiles con Huevo, Estilo de Casa
variations.en: Soft chilaquiles with red chile and eggs
variations.note: How a lot of Mexican-American families make them: store-bought or same-morning tortillas fried soft, not crunchy like chips, then cooked in the pan with red chile and eggs.

items: 10–12 corn tortillas, store-bought or homemade, cut or torn into strips or pieces
1½ cups red chile (below), or leftover enchilada chile or salsa
For the red chile: 6 dried New Mexico, California or guajillo chiles
To serve: shredded cheese or queso fresco, frijoles, warm tortillas

steps: Make the chile: stem and seed the chiles, simmer them in the water 10 minutes, then blend with the garlic, cumin, oregano and salt. Strain.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Fry the tortilla pieces, stirring, 3–4 minutes, until golden in spots but still soft and a little chewy. Pour off extra oil.
For eggs fried first: push the tortillas to the side, crack the eggs into the pan and let them fry a minute until the whites start to set. Then break them up and mix them through the tortillas.
For scrambled: beat the eggs with a pinch of salt, pour them over the tortillas and stir until just set.
Pour in the chile and toss everything together. Simmer 1–2 minutes, until the tortillas soak it up.
Top with cheese and serve with beans and tortillas.

variations.name: Chilaquiles Rojos
variations.note: The same method with a red salsa of tomato and dried chiles.

items: 3 chiles guajillo and 2 chiles de árbol, toasted and soaked
1 garlic clove, ¼ onion and 1 cup broth

steps: Blend the tomatoes, chiles, garlic, onion and broth, and strain.
Fry the salsa 5 minutes and season.
Toss with the totopos and top as in the base.

recipes.verso: Maíz que revienta en flor: el pozole del quince, ¡qué sabor!
recipes.name: Pozole Rojo
recipes.story: Pozole goes back to pre-Hispanic Mexico, when cacahuazintle corn was cooked for ceremonies. In Jalisco it's red with guajillo and ancho, made with pork head or a mix of shoulder and bony cuts. It's what you make for 15 de septiembre, Nochebuena and New Year's. The broth should be brick red and thin, never a thick chili, and the garnish happens at the table.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 2 lb pork neck bones or spine (espinazo)
2 pig's feet (manitas), split, optional but they give body
1 tbsp salt, plus more to taste

ingredients.title: El maíz
items: 2 lb precooked cacahuazintle hominy (maíz pozolero, sold in bags at Mexican markets), rinsed, or 2 cans (29 oz each) hominy, drained and rinsed

ingredients.title: El chile
items: 1–2 chiles de árbol, optional, for heat
Pinch of cumin, only if your family uses it

ingredients.title: Para servir
items: Finely shredded green cabbage, or lettuce as many tapatíos prefer

steps: Put the meats, onion and garlic in your biggest pot with the water. Bring to a boil and skim the gray foam for the first 15 minutes so the broth stays clean.

If using bagged hominy, add it now. Lower to a gentle simmer, partly covered, and cook 2 to 2½ hours, until the meat is very tender and the kernels have opened like flowers (revienta). Add the salt only once the corn has bloomed; salting early keeps it hard.
Meanwhile, stem and seed the chiles. Toast them on a hot comal 10–20 seconds per side, just until fragrant and pliable. Cover with hot water and soak 15 minutes.
Blend the chiles with the garlic, onion, oregano, cumin (if using) and 1½ cups of the pork broth until completely smooth. Pour through a fine strainer, pressing with a spoon. Discard the skins.
Lift out the meat. Shred or cut it into bite-size pieces, pick the meat off the bones and feet, and return it to the pot. Discard bones, onion and garlic.
If using canned hominy, add it now. Stir in the strained chile and simmer 30 minutes. Season well with salt. It should be red and brothy, not thick.
Serve in deep bowls. Everyone garnishes their own: cabbage, radish, onion, oregano rubbed between the palms, chile piquín and a good squeeze of lime. Tostadas on the side.

pressureCooker.time: 45 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Toast, soak, blend and strain the chiles exactly as in the traditional method.
Put the meats, onion and garlic in the pot. Add bagged hominy now if using. Add water to the max-fill line (about 3½ quarts in an 8-qt pot; use about two-thirds of the meat in a 6-qt).
Seal and cook at high pressure 45 minutes (55 if using pig's feet). Let the pressure release naturally for 20 minutes, then vent.
Remove the meat, shred it, discard the bones and aromatics, and return the meat.
Switch to Sauté. Add the strained chile, canned hominy if using, and the salt (salt after the corn has bloomed). Simmer uncovered 20–30 minutes. Taste and serve.
pressureCooker.note: Plenty of abuelas already make pozole in a stovetop olla exprés. Count about 35 minutes from when the valve starts to rock.

tips: Strain the chile. The skins make the broth gritty and bitter.
Toast chiles until you smell them, only seconds. If they smoke, they'll taste bitter: throw them out and start over.
Pozole is better the next day. Chill it and lift off the fat if you like.
A weeknight version most families accept: bone-in chicken thighs instead of pork, about 1 hour on the stove.

variations.name: Pozole Verde
variations.note: Thursdays in Guerrero are jueves pozolero. The green comes from pepitas, tomatillo and fresh herbs. The table gets chicharrón and avocado and, depending on the region, a raw egg cracked into the hot broth or sardines, with mezcal on the side.

items: Pork and hominy from the base recipe (or 1 whole chicken)
2 hoja santa leaves (or 1 tsp anise seed)
To serve: chicharrón, avocado, onion, oregano, lime, tostadas

steps: Cook the meat and hominy as in the base recipe, steps 1, 2 and 5 (add canned hominy now if using). Leave out the red chile.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan, stirring, until they puff and pop but don't brown. Let cool.
Simmer the tomatillos and chiles in water 8 minutes, until olive green. Drain.
Blend the pepitas, tomatillos, chiles, onion, garlic, hoja santa, epazote, cilantro and romaine or radish leaves with 2 cups broth until very smooth.
Heat the lard in a skillet and fry the green sauce 5 minutes, stirring.
Stir it into the pot and keep at a bare simmer 15 minutes. A hard boil makes the pepita sauce split.
Serve with the garnishes.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure times for the meat. Add the green sauce on Sauté-Low and don't let it boil.

variations.name: Pozole Blanco
variations.note: The oldest style: pork, corn and salt in the broth, nothing else. All the chile is served on the side so each bowl is seasoned at the table.

items: Everything from the base recipe except the red chile
For the salsa: 10 chiles de árbol

steps: Cook the meat and hominy as in the base, steps 1, 2 and 5 (add canned hominy now if using). Skip the chile.
For the salsa, toast the chiles a few seconds, soak 10 minutes, blend with garlic, salt and water, and strain.
Serve the white broth with the salsa, onion, oregano, lime, cabbage and radish on the table.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure times as the base recipe.

recipes.verso: Al dolor de cabeza, el comer le endereza.
recipes.name: Menudo Rojo
recipes.story: Sunday morning menudo, el levantamuertos, is the norteño cure for a long Saturday night. In central Mexico the same soup is pancita, and in Yucatán mondongo. The tripe is cleaned with lime and cooked slowly with pata de res, the beef foot that makes the broth sticky. Families start it on Saturday so it's ready for breakfast.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 2 lb beef foot (pata de res), cut in pieces by the butcher
2 limes or ¼ cup white vinegar, plus a handful of coarse salt, for cleaning

ingredients.title: El maíz
items: 1 can (29 oz) hominy, drained and rinsed

steps: Clean the tripe: rinse it, rub it all over with lime halves (or vinegar) and a handful of salt, and rinse again under cold water. Trim excess fat and cut into 1½-inch squares.
Put the beef foot, tripe, onion and garlic in a large pot with the water. Bring to a boil and skim for 15 minutes.
Lower to a gentle simmer, partly covered, and cook 3½–4 hours. The tripe is ready when it's tender with a little chew and the beef foot is soft and gelatinous. Add hot water if it reduces too much.
Toast, soak and blend the chiles with the garlic, oregano, cumin and 1½ cups broth. Strain into the pot.
Add the hominy and salt. Simmer 30 minutes more. Pick the meat off the foot bones if you like, and discard the bones and aromatics.
Serve very hot with onion, oregano, chile piquín, lime and tortillas.

pressureCooker.time: 60 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Clean and cut the tripe as in step 1.
Put the tripe, beef foot, onion, garlic and salt in the pot. Add water to the max-fill line.
Meanwhile, toast, soak, blend and strain the chiles as in step 4.
High pressure 60 minutes. Natural release 20 minutes. If the tripe is still tough, seal again for 15 minutes.
Add the strained chile and the hominy. Simmer on Sauté 20 minutes.
pressureCooker.note: Tripe varies a lot. Pre-cooked white tripe from the store needs only about 30 minutes.

tips: The pata is what makes your lips stick together. Don't skip it.
Lime and salt take away the barnyard smell. Rinse until the water runs clear.
Make it a day ahead. The fat sets on top and lifts right off.

variations.name: Menudo Blanco
variations.note: In Sonora and Sinaloa menudo is white by default: no chile in the pot, and the heat comes from crushed chiltepín at the table, with buttered birote or bolillo.

items: Everything from the base recipe except the chile

steps: Cook the tripe and beef foot as in the base, steps 1–3.
Add the hominy and salt and simmer 30 minutes.
Serve with chiltepín, oregano, onion, cilantro and lime.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure time as the base.

recipes.verso: Caldo de res con su hueso: el que lo prueba regresa por eso.
recipes.name: Caldo de Res
recipes.story: The everyday soup of every Mexican home: beef shank with the bone and marrow, corn on the cob and whatever vegetables the market has. The rice goes in the bowl, not the pot.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 3 lb beef shank (chambarete), bone-in with marrow
1 lb beef short ribs (costilla de res), optional

ingredients.title: Las verduras
items: 3 ears of corn, each cut in 3 rounds
1 chayote, peeled and cut in wedges

steps: Put the meat, onion and garlic in a big pot with the water. Bring to a boil and skim the foam for 15 minutes.
Add the salt, lower the heat and simmer partly covered 2 hours, until the meat is tender.
Blend the tomatoes with a cup of broth and strain into the pot. It gives the caldo a light color.
Add the vegetables by how long they take: corn and carrots first, 15 minutes; then potatoes and chayote, 10 minutes; then zucchini and cabbage, 8 minutes.
Turn off the heat and drop in the cilantro and mint. Taste for salt.
Put a spoon of arroz rojo in each bowl, add meat and vegetables, and ladle the broth over. Lime and chile at the table.

pressureCooker.time: 40 min high pressure + 15 min natural release
steps: Put the meat, onion, garlic, salt and 3 quarts water in the pot. High pressure 40 minutes, natural release 15.
Add the strained tomato, corn, carrots, potatoes and chayote. High pressure 3 minutes, quick release.
Switch to Sauté, add the zucchini and cabbage, and simmer 5 minutes. Add the cilantro and mint off the heat.

tips: Scoop the marrow out of the bone onto a hot tortilla with salt and salsa. That's the cook's reward.
Mint is the quiet secret in a lot of family caldos. One sprig is enough.

variations.name: Mole de Olla
variations.note: Caldo de res's spicier cousin. The broth is tinted with dried chiles and soured with xoconostle, a tart cactus fruit. Many central families drop in chochoyotes, little masa-and-epazote dumplings pressed with a thumb, for the last 10 minutes. The saying «¡A darle, que es mole de olla!» means let's get to it.

items: Meat and broth from the base, steps 1–2
4 chiles guajillo, 2 chiles pasilla (1 ancho, optional)
2 Roma tomatoes, 2 garlic cloves, ¼ onion
2 xoconostles, peeled, seeded and quartered (or the juice of 1 lime at the end)

steps: Cook the meat as in the base.
Toast and soak the chiles. Blend with the tomatoes, garlic and onion, strain, and fry in the lard 5 minutes.
Add the chile to the broth with the corn, potatoes, chayote and xoconostle. Cook 15 minutes.
Add the green beans, zucchini and epazote and cook 8 minutes more.
Serve with chopped onion, serrano and lime.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure steps as the base. Add the fried chile with the first batch of vegetables.

recipes.verso: Pa' la gripa y pa'l desamor, un caldito es lo mejor.
recipes.name: Caldo de Pollo
recipes.story: The soup for colds, for heartbreak and for Sundays. Abuela used a gallina, an old laying hen with more flavor than a young chicken. The broth should be clear and golden.

ingredients.title: El caldo
items: 1 whole chicken (or stewing hen), cut in pieces, skin on

ingredients.title: Para servir
items: Limes, chopped onion and cilantro, serrano

steps: Put the chicken, onion, garlic, tomato and celery in a pot with the water. Bring to a boil and skim well.
Add the salt and simmer gently 40 minutes (1½–2 hours for a hen). Keep it at a lazy bubble so the broth stays clear.
Remove the tomato and onion. Add the carrots and potatoes and cook 10 minutes. Add the chayote, zucchini and chickpeas and cook 8 minutes.
Add the cilantro off the heat. Serve with lime, onion, chile, avocado and rice.

pressureCooker.time: 15 min high pressure + 10 min natural release
steps: Put the chicken, aromatics, salt and 2½ quarts water in the pot. High pressure 15 minutes (30 for a hen), natural release 10.
Remove the aromatics. Add the carrots, potatoes and chayote. High pressure 2 minutes, quick release.
On Sauté, add the zucchini and chickpeas for 4 minutes. Finish with cilantro.

tips: Once the foam is skimmed, never let it boil hard or the broth turns cloudy.
Add a handful of rice or fideo to the pot for a heartier soup.

variations.name: Caldo Tlalpeño
variations.note: A chipotle chicken soup named for Tlalpan, in the south of the capital. Local legend says it was made for Santa Anna as a hangover cure, and Tlalpan still holds a Festival del Caldo Tlalpeño.

items: Broth and shredded chicken from the base
2 chipotles en adobo (or 2 dried chipotles, toasted and soaked)
2 Roma tomatoes, ¼ onion, 1 garlic clove
2 carrots, diced, and ½ lb green beans, cut
To serve: avocado, cubes of queso panela or Oaxaca, lime

steps: Shred the chicken from the base, discarding the skin and bones. Blend the tomatoes, onion, garlic and chipotle with a cup of broth and fry in the oil 5 minutes.
Add to the broth with the carrots and chickpeas and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the green beans, epazote and shredded chicken and simmer 5 minutes.
Serve over cubes of cheese and avocado, with lime.
variations.pressureNote: Use the base pressure steps and add the chipotle sauce with the carrots.

recipes.verso: Fideo dorado, nunca quemado.
recipes.name: Sopa de Fideo
recipes.en: Toasted noodle soup in tomato broth
recipes.story: The first soup most Mexican kids learn to love. Everything depends on toasting the noodles to the color of a peanut shell before the tomato goes in.

ingredients.title: Sopa
items: 1 sprig cilantro (or a few leaves of epazote)

steps: Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic with 1 cup of the broth until smooth.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium. Add the fideo, breaking up the coils, and stir constantly until deep golden. Don't walk away; it burns fast.
Pour the tomato purée through a strainer into the pot. It will sizzle. Fry, stirring, 3 minutes until it darkens.
Add the rest of the broth, the salt and the cilantro. Simmer 8–10 minutes, until the fideo is soft.
Serve with lime, and crema and queso if you like.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. This soup is done in 30 minutes on the stove, and the noodles would turn to mush.
tips: If the fideo browns too fast, pull the pot off the heat. It keeps cooking in the hot oil.

variations.name: Sopa Seca de Fideo
variations.note: A dry soup, cooked until the noodles absorb all the broth. It's the second tiempo of a comida corrida: sopa aguada, then sopa seca, then the guisado.

items: Same as the base, but only 3 cups broth (1 for the purée, 2 to cook)
1–2 chipotles en adobo, blended with the tomato

steps: Toast the fideo and fry the tomato-chipotle purée as in the base.
Add 2 cups broth, cover and cook on low 10 minutes until absorbed.
Top with crema, queso and avocado.

recipes.verso: Con su arroz y su hierbabuena, la albóndiga sale buena.
recipes.name: Albóndigas en Caldillo
recipes.story: Mexican meatballs carry raw rice inside, which swells as they cook and keeps them tender, and fresh mint, which is the flavor everyone remembers.

ingredients.title: Albóndigas
items: ¼ cup long-grain rice, soaked 15 minutes in hot water and drained
1 tsp salt and ¼ tsp black pepper

ingredients.title: Caldillo
items: 8 cups beef or chicken broth (or water)

steps: Mix all the albóndiga ingredients with your hands just until combined. Wet your hands and roll balls the size of a golf ball.
Blend the tomatoes, onion, garlic and chipotle. Heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the purée 5 minutes, until it darkens.
Add the broth and the mint sprig. Bring to a boil and add the carrots and potato.
Lower in the meatballs one at a time. Don't stir for the first 10 minutes so they can set.
Simmer 25–30 minutes, adding the zucchini for the last 10. Taste for salt.
Serve with tortillas and lime.

pressureCooker.time: 8 min high pressure + 10 min natural release
steps: On Sauté, fry the tomato purée 5 minutes.
Add the broth, mint, carrots and potato. Gently set in the meatballs.
High pressure 8 minutes, natural release 10.
Add the zucchini and simmer on Sauté 3 minutes.

tips: Some families tuck a piece of hard-boiled egg inside each meatball. Kids love finding it.
Keep your hands wet while rolling and the meat won't stick.

recipes.verso: Dicen que birria es cosa sin valor… ¡pero en Jalisco es puro sabor!
recipes.name: Birria de Chivo
recipes.en: Goat in chile adobo with consomé
recipes.story: Birria comes from Jalisco, where goat was cooked in a pit or in a pot sealed shut with masa. The adobo is dried chiles, vinegar and warm spices, and the meat is served in a bowl of its own consomé. 'Birria' means something worthless: popular history says the Spaniards scorned goat, and Jalisco (Cocula claims the honor) turned it into a feast.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 5 lb bone-in goat (or lamb shoulder, or a mix of beef chuck and short rib)

ingredients.title: El consomé
items: 2 cups water, plus more for the consomé (about 6 cups in all)

steps: Stem and seed the chiles. Toast them on a comal a few seconds per side and soak in hot water 15 minutes.
Toast the cumin, cloves, peppercorns and cinnamon in a dry pan for 30 seconds.
Blend the chiles with the vinegar, spices, garlic, onion, oregano, ginger, thyme, marjoram and salt, adding just enough soaking water to make a thick paste.
Rub the paste all over the meat. Cover and refrigerate overnight, or at least 4 hours.

Put a rack in a large Dutch oven with 2 cups water and the bay leaves underneath. Set the meat on the rack and scrape in all the adobo. Cover with foil and then the lid, sealing as tightly as you can. That's the home version of sealing the pot with masa.
Cook in a 325°F oven 3½–4 hours, until the meat falls off the bone.

Lift out the meat. Skim the red fat from the juices and save it. Blend the charred tomatoes with some of the juices, add them back, add water to make about 6 cups of consomé, and simmer 10 minutes. Season.
Serve the meat in bowls with hot consomé, onion, cilantro, oregano, lime, salsa and tortillas.

pressureCooker.time: 50 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Make the adobo and marinate as in steps 1–4.
Put the meat, all the adobo, the bay leaves and 2 cups water in the pot.
High pressure 50 minutes for goat or lamb, 60 for beef chuck. Natural release 20 minutes.
Lift out the meat. Skim and save the fat. Blend in the tomatoes and simmer the consomé on Sauté 10 minutes.
pressureCooker.note: Don't skip the overnight marinade. The pressure cooker saves cooking time, not flavor time.

tips: Save the red fat from the top of the consomé to fry tortillas for tacos.
The vinegar matters. It cuts the richness and helps tenderize the meat.
Birria tatemada: brown the drained meat in a hot oven or on the comal for roasted edges before serving.

variations.name: Birria de Res estilo Tijuana
variations.note: The version that took over social media: the same adobo with beef, and tacos crisped in the red fat with melted cheese, dipped in consomé. Not the abuela original, but nobody complains.

items: Adobo and consomé from the base
2 lb beef chuck, 2 lb short ribs, 1 lb oxtail

steps: Marinate and cook the beef as in the base (4 hours in the oven or 60 minutes under pressure).
Shred the meat and keep the consomé hot.
Dip a tortilla in the red fat, lay it on a hot griddle, add cheese and meat, fold, and cook until crisp on both sides.
Serve with a cup of consomé topped with onion and cilantro for dipping.

recipes.verso: En hoja de plátano envuelta, sale la cochinita bien suelta.
recipes.name: Cochinita Pibil
recipes.story: Pibil means cooked in the pib, the Maya earth oven. Pork marinates in achiote and sour orange, then cooks wrapped in banana leaves until it falls apart. In Mérida it's breakfast, eaten in tacos and tortas.

ingredients.title: El recado
items: 1 cup naranja agria (sour orange) juice, or ⅔ cup orange juice plus ⅓ cup lime juice

steps: Blend the achiote with the juice, garlic, salt and spices until smooth.
Coat the pork with it and marinate overnight, covered, in the fridge.
Pass the banana leaves quickly over a flame or burner until they turn shiny and soft. Line a Dutch oven or deep baking dish with them, letting them hang over the sides.
Add the pork and all the marinade, dot with the lard, and fold the leaves over to close the package. Cover with foil and the lid.
Bake at 325°F for 3½–4 hours, until the pork pulls apart with a fork.
Open the leaves and shred the pork in its juices. Serve with pickled onion and habanero salsa.

pressureCooker.time: 50 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Marinate the pork overnight.
Line the pot with softened banana leaves. Add the pork, the marinade and ½ cup water, and fold the leaves over.
High pressure 50 minutes, natural release 20.
Shred the pork. If the juices are thin, lift out the meat and reduce them on Sauté 5 minutes.

tips: Seville oranges (naranja agria) are the real thing. Latin markets sell the juice bottled if you can't find fresh.
For tortas de cochinita, split a bolillo and fill it with pork, onions and a spoon of the juices. That's breakfast in Mérida.

variations.name: Cebolla Morada Encurtida
variations.note: Always on the table with cochinita.

items: 1 habanero, thinly sliced (seeds out for less heat)
½ cup naranja agria or lime juice

steps: Pour boiling water over the onions, wait 10 seconds and drain. It softens the bite and turns them bright pink.
Toss with the habanero, juice, salt and oregano.
Let stand at least 1 hour. Keeps a week in the fridge.

variations.name: Xnipec
variations.note: Its Maya name means dog's nose, because it's spicy enough to make your nose wet.
steps: Mix everything and let it sit 15 minutes before serving.

recipes.verso: En el cazo de cobre, la carnita nunca es pobre.
recipes.name: Carnitas
recipes.story: In Quiroga, Michoacán, the carnitas capital, they're made in big copper cazos from Santa Clara del Cobre, the pork simmering in lard until it's tender inside and crisp outside. Orange and a splash of milk or Coke help it brown. It's party food for weekends, baptisms and birthdays.

ingredients.title: Carnitas
items: 5 lb pork shoulder, in 3-inch chunks (add some ribs or skin if you can)
2 lb lard (manteca), enough to almost cover
½ cup whole milk or Mexican Coca-Cola, optional

steps: Melt the lard in a heavy pot (cast iron or Dutch oven) over medium heat.
Add the pork, the salt, and the garlic and herbs if using. The lard should bubble gently, not fry hard. Cook 2 hours, stirring now and then, until the meat is tender.
Squeeze in the orange and drop in the halves. Add the milk or Coke. Cook 15 minutes.
Raise the heat to medium-high for the last 15–20 minutes so the pork turns golden brown and crisp at the edges. Watch for splatter.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain. Chop and serve with tortillas, salsa, onion, cilantro and lime.
Strain the lard when it cools and keep it in the fridge. It's gold for beans and tamales.

pressureCooker.time: 40 min high pressure + 15 min natural release, then broil
steps: Put the pork, salt, orange juice and halves, garlic, bay leaves, ½ cup water and 3 tbsp lard in the pot.
High pressure 40 minutes, natural release 15.
Spread the meat on a sheet pan, break it into chunks, and drizzle with a few spoons of the fat and juices.
Broil 5–8 minutes until the edges crisp, or fry in batches in a hot cast-iron pan with lard.

tips: Ask the carnicero for carnitas surtidas: maciza (lean), cuerito (skin), costilla (rib) and buche (stomach).
Don't stir much at first. Let the pork confit quietly.
Purists use only lard, salt and time. Orange, milk and Coca-Cola are carnitero tricks for color, and every one has his own fórmula. If you use Coke, make it the cane-sugar Mexican one.

recipes.verso: Domingo sin barbacoa, domingo que no se goza.
recipes.name: Barbacoa de Res
recipes.story: In Hidalgo, barbacoa is lamb wrapped in maguey leaves and cooked overnight in a pit, with a pot underneath catching the juices for consomé. This home version steams beef with avocado leaves. Barbacoa is el almuerzo dominguero: in the north, families buy cachete, lengua and cabeza by the kilo on Sunday mornings.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 3 lb beef cheeks (cachete), or chuck roast in large pieces
6 dried avocado leaves, toasted (or 1 tsp anise seed)

ingredients.title: Consomé
items: Chopped onion, cilantro, lime and salsa

steps: Rub the meat with the salt, pepper, cumin and garlic. Let stand 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.
Put a rack or steamer basket in a tall pot with 4 cups water, the onion and the bay leaves underneath.
Lay banana leaves on the rack if you have them, add the avocado leaves and the meat, and fold the banana leaves over.
Cover tightly and steam on low 4–5 hours, adding hot water when needed, until the meat shreds easily.
Shred the meat. For the consomé, strain the liquid from under the rack, add the chickpeas, rice and carrot, and simmer 20 minutes.
Serve the barbacoa in tortillas with salsa, and the consomé in a cup on the side with chopped onion, cilantro and lime.

pressureCooker.time: 65 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Season the meat. Put the onion, bay leaves, avocado leaves and 1½ cups water in the pot and add the meat.
High pressure 65 minutes, natural release 20.
Shred the meat with a little of the liquid.
Strain the remaining liquid, add the chickpeas, rice and carrot, and cook on Sauté 15 minutes for consomé.

tips: Mexican avocado leaves taste of anise. Toast them a few seconds on the comal before using.
Cheeks are full of collagen. Don't trim them too lean or you'll lose the silky texture.

variations.name: Salsa Borracha
variations.en: Pasilla salsa with beer or pulque
variations.note: The classic partner for barbacoa, traditionally made with pulque.

items: ½ cup pulque or light Mexican beer
Crumbled queso añejo and chopped onion, to finish

steps: Toast the pasillas briefly and soak 10 minutes.
Grind in the molcajete or blend with the garlic, onion, beer and salt. Keep it a little coarse.
Top with queso añejo and chopped onion.

recipes.verso: Puerco, tomate y verdolaga: la comida que no empalaga.
recipes.name: Puerco en Salsa Verde
recipes.en: Pork in tomatillo salsa with purslane
recipes.story: A weekday guisado. The pork cooks in a little water until the water is gone and it fries in its own fat, and then the salsa goes in. Verdolagas (purslane) add a lemony, juicy bite. Potatoes or nopales are just as common.

ingredients.title: El puerco
items: 2½ lb pork shoulder or country ribs, in 1½-inch pieces

ingredients.title: La verdura
items: 1 lb verdolagas (purslane), thick stems removed, or 3 potatoes, cubed, or 2 cups cooked nopales

steps: Put the pork, water and salt in a wide pan. Cook uncovered over medium, stirring now and then, until the water is gone and the pork browns in its own fat, about 40 minutes. Add the lard if the pork is lean.
Meanwhile, simmer the tomatillos and serranos in water 8 minutes, until they turn olive green. Drain.
Blend them with the onion, garlic, cilantro and cumin.
Pour the salsa over the pork. It will sizzle. Season and simmer 20 minutes, until slightly thickened. (Potatoes go in now.)
Blanch the verdolagas 1 minute in boiling water, drain, and stir them into the pot for the last 5 minutes (or add the cooked nopales).
Serve with frijoles and tortillas.

pressureCooker.time: 20 min high pressure + 10 min natural release
steps: Brown the pork in the lard on Sauté, in batches.
Blend the raw tomatillos, serranos, onion, garlic and cumin (no need to boil them first). Pour over the pork with ½ cup water. Add potatoes now if using.
High pressure 20 minutes, natural release 10.
Stir in the blanched verdolagas and the cilantro and simmer on Sauté 5 minutes.

tips: Don't over-boil tomatillos. As soon as they turn from bright to olive green, take them out, or they burst and turn sour.
Purslane grows wild in a lot of gardens. It's free food.

recipes.verso: Tinga en tostada, la fiesta está armada.
recipes.name: Tinga de Pollo
recipes.story: Tinga is from Puebla: lots of soft onion, tomato and smoky chipotle. It goes on tostadas with beans, crema and queso, and it's what you bring to a fiesta. Tostadas de tinga are on nearly every table at the Noche Mexicana on 15 de septiembre, next to the pozole.

ingredients.title: El pollo
items: ¼ onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1 bay leaf and salt, for poaching

ingredients.title: La salsa
items: 2–4 chipotles en adobo, plus 1 tbsp of the adobo sauce

steps: Simmer the chicken in water with the onion, garlic, bay leaf and salt for 20 minutes. Cool, shred and save 1 cup of the broth.
Blend the tomatoes with the chipotles and adobo sauce.
Heat the lard and cook the sliced onions over medium-low 8 minutes, until soft and translucent but not brown. Add the garlic for 1 minute.
Add the tomato-chipotle purée, oregano and bay leaves. Cook 8 minutes, until it darkens.
Add the chicken and ½ cup of the broth. Simmer 10 minutes until juicy but not soupy. Season.
Spread tostadas with beans, pile on the tinga, and top with lettuce, crema, queso and avocado.

pressureCooker.time: 10 min high pressure + 5 min natural release
steps: On Sauté, soften the onions in the lard, then add the garlic.
Add the purée, oregano, bay leaves and ½ cup water. Nestle in the raw chicken thighs.
High pressure 10 minutes (8 for breasts), natural release 5.
Shred the chicken right in the sauce. Simmer on Sauté a few minutes to thicken.

tips: Be generous with the onion. Tinga should be half onion.
Start with 2 chipotles and add more after tasting. The heat varies from can to can.

variations.name: Tinga Poblana de Puerco
variations.note: The oldest printed tingas (La cocinera poblana, 1881) are pork with chorizo and longaniza, sometimes with potato.

items: 2 lb pork shoulder, cooked and shredded
The same tinga sauce as the base

steps: Fry the chorizo until it releases its fat. Add the onions and cook until soft.
Add the tomato-chipotle purée and cook 8 minutes, then add the pork and potato.
Simmer 10 minutes. Serve on tostadas with avocado.
variations.pressureNote: Cook the pork shoulder chunks at high pressure 35 minutes, natural release 10, then shred.

recipes.verso: Picadillo de la abuela: rinde, llena y consuela.
recipes.name: Picadillo
recipes.en: Ground beef with potato and carrot
recipes.story: Ground meat cooked with tomato, potato and carrot. Every family has its own, and it fills tacos dorados, gorditas, empanadas and chiles rellenos.

ingredients.title: Picadillo
items: 1½ lb ground beef (or half beef, half pork)
1 tsp salt and ¼ tsp pepper

steps: Brown the meat in the oil, breaking it up, until no pink remains. Spoon off the extra fat.
Add the onion, garlic and serrano and cook 3 minutes.
Add the tomato, cumin, salt and pepper and cook 5 minutes.
Add the potatoes, carrots and water. Cover and simmer 15 minutes until tender, adding the peas for the last 5.
Serve with rice, beans and tortillas, or use it as a filling.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Picadillo is done in 40 minutes in a skillet, and the browning is where the flavor comes from.
tips: Cut the potatoes and carrots small, about the size of a pea, so every bite gets some.

variations.name: Picadillo de Fiesta
variations.note: The fruit-and-nut filling for chiles en nogada, made July to September when the orchards around Puebla bear fruit. More work, and very good.

items: 1 lb ground pork plus ½ lb ground beef
½ onion and 2 garlic cloves, chopped; 3 tomatoes, blended
1 ripe plantain, 1 pear (pera de leche), 1 peach (durazno criollo) and 1 apple (manzana panochera), all diced small
¼ cup raisins and ¼ cup slivered almonds
¼ cup candied pineapple (real acitrón comes from a protected cactus)
½ tsp cinnamon and a pinch of cloves

steps: Brown the meat with the onion and garlic.
Add the tomato and cook 5 minutes.
Add the apple first, then the pear and peach, then the plantain, nuts, raisins, candied fruit and spices. Cook 15 minutes, until the fruit is tender but holds its shape.
Season with salt and a little sugar. Use to stuff roasted poblanos.

recipes.verso: Capeado como Dios manda: esponjadito y sin grasa.
recipes.name: Chiles Rellenos
recipes.story: Roasted poblanos stuffed with cheese, wrapped in a fluffy egg batter, fried, and served in a thin tomato broth. They take patience. Abuela's are light and puffy, never greasy.

ingredients.title: Chiles
items: 6 large poblano chiles, flat and straight
12 oz queso Oaxaca, Chihuahua or asadero, cut in sticks

ingredients.title: Capeado (batter)
items: Oil for frying, about 1 inch deep

steps: Roast the poblanos directly over a gas flame (or under the broiler), turning, until blackened all over.
Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate or a plastic bag, and let them sweat 10 minutes.
Peel off the charred skin with your fingers. Don't rinse them, or you'll wash away the flavor. Cut a slit down one side and carefully pull out the seeds, leaving the stem on.
Stuff each chile with cheese and close the slit with a toothpick.
Make the caldillo: blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic, fry in the oil 5 minutes, add the broth and bay leaf, and simmer 10 minutes. It should be thin. Season.
Beat the egg whites with the salt to stiff peaks. Beat in the yolks one at a time, just until mixed.
Heat the oil to 350°F. Dust each chile with flour, shake off the extra, and dip in the batter to coat.
Fry 2–3 minutes per side, spooning hot oil over the top, until golden. Drain on paper towels and pull out the toothpicks.
Set the chiles in the hot caldillo for a minute and serve with arroz rojo and frijoles.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. This one belongs to the open flame and the skillet.
tips: The flour is what makes the batter stick. Don't skip it.
Pick poblanos that are smooth and flat. They roast and peel evenly.

variations.name: Rellenos de Picadillo
variations.note: Stuffed with picadillo instead of cheese.

items: Batter and caldillo from the base

steps: Fill the chiles with picadillo instead of cheese.
Batter, fry and serve in caldillo as in the base.

recipes.verso: ¡Aquí sí estamos en nuestro mero mole!
recipes.name: Mole Poblano
recipes.en: Chile, chocolate and spice sauce with turkey
recipes.story: Mole poblano is the dish for weddings, baptisms and Día de Muertos. Dozens of ingredients, each one fried or toasted on its own, then ground together and cooked slowly until the fat rises to the top. Abuelas make it in big batches with the whole family helping. Puebla's legend credits Sor Andrea de la Asunción at the Convento de Santa Rosa around 1680, though no document proves it.

ingredients.title: La carne
items: 1 white onion, 1 head garlic and salt
About 10 cups of the cooking broth

ingredients.title: Los chiles
items: 1 tbsp of the chile seeds, saved

ingredients.title: Semillas y frutas
items: ⅓ cup sesame seeds, plus more for garnish
1 slice day-old bolillo or white bread

ingredients.title: Lo demás
items: ½ white onion and 4 garlic cloves, charred

steps: Simmer the turkey with the onion, garlic and salt until tender, about 1½ hours (40 minutes for chicken). Keep the broth.
Stem and seed the chiles, saving 1 tbsp of seeds. Fry the chiles a few seconds per side in hot lard, just until they blister and change color. Soak in hot broth 30 minutes.
In the same lard, fry each of these separately and set aside: almonds, peanuts, pepitas, raisins (until they puff), plantain (until dark golden), tortilla (until crisp) and bread (until golden).
On a dry comal, toast the sesame until golden, the saved chile seeds until very dark, and the spices for 30 seconds.
Blend the chiles with enough soaking liquid to make a smooth purée.
Blend the nuts, seeds, fruit, tortilla, bread, spices, tomatoes, tomatillos, onion and garlic with broth, in batches, until completely smooth. Strain both purées if you want a silky mole.

Heat 3 tbsp lard in a large heavy pot or cazuela until very hot. Pour in the chile purée all at once (stand back, it splatters). Fry it, stirring constantly, 15 minutes until it darkens and thickens. This is called frying the mole.
Add the nut purée and cook 20 minutes, stirring often.
Add the chocolate, sugar and salt, and enough broth that it coats the back of a spoon. Simmer on low 45–60 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't stick, until a sheen of fat rises to the surface.
Add the turkey and heat through. Serve with sesame seeds, arroz rojo and tortillas.

pressureCooker.time: Turkey: 25 min high pressure + 15 min natural release
steps: Pressure-cook the turkey pieces with the onion, garlic, salt and water to the fill line: high pressure 25 minutes (12 for chicken), natural release 15. Keep the broth.
Make the mole sauce on the stove as in steps 2–9. The frying and slow simmer can't be rushed under pressure, and a thick mole will set off the burn warning.
pressureCooker.note: The sauce still takes about 2 hours on the stove. Make a big batch of the fried mole paste; it freezes for months.

tips: Mole is better on the second day.
Many poblano families take the fried chiles and seeds to the neighborhood molino to be ground.
If you use store-bought mole paste, fry it in lard first, then thin it with broth and add a piece of Mexican chocolate. Not abuela's, but honest.
The fat rising to the top is how you know it's done.

variations.name: Pipián Verde
variations.note: A pre-Hispanic green mole thickened with pepitas instead of nuts and dried chiles. Lighter and quicker than mole poblano. Many cooks call nearly the same dish mole verde.

items: 2 lb chicken pieces, poached, plus the broth
1 sprig epazote, 2 hoja santa leaves and a handful of cilantro

steps: Toast the pepitas until they pop but don't brown. Let cool.
Simmer the tomatillos and serranos 8 minutes and drain.
Blend everything except the chicken, lard and salt with 2 cups broth until very smooth.
Fry the sauce in the lard over medium 5 minutes, stirring, then thin with broth.
Simmer gently 15 minutes, never at a hard boil or it will split. Add the chicken and season.
variations.pressureNote: Cook the chicken at high pressure 12 minutes, natural release 10. Make the sauce on the stove.

recipes.verso: El que nace pa' tamal, del cielo le caen las hojas.
recipes.name: Tamales Rojos de Puerco
recipes.story: Tamales are a group effort. The tamalada, usually before Christmas, puts the whole family at the table spreading masa. Red pork tamales are the classic.

ingredients.title: El relleno
items: 2½ lb pork shoulder, in large chunks
½ onion, 3 garlic cloves and 1 tbsp salt
2 garlic cloves, ½ tsp cumin and ½ tsp Mexican oregano

ingredients.title: La masa
items: 4 lb fresh unprepared masa for tamales (from a tortillería), or 6 cups masa harina for tamales mixed with about 5 cups warm broth
2 cups (450 g) fresh pork lard, not hydrogenated
½ cup of the red chile sauce, for color

ingredients.title: Las hojas
items: 60 dried corn husks, soaked in hot water 1 hour

steps: Cover the pork with water, add the onion, garlic and salt, and simmer 2 hours until tender. Shred and keep the broth.
Toast, soak and blend the chiles with the garlic, cumin, oregano and 1½ cups broth. Strain.
Fry the sauce in the lard 5 minutes. Set aside ½ cup for the masa. Add the pork to the rest and simmer 15 minutes until thick, not soupy. Let cool.
Beat the lard with a mixer 3–5 minutes until white and fluffy.
Add the masa a handful at a time, alternating with the broth, baking powder, salt and reserved chile. Beat 10 minutes. It should feel like soft peanut butter.
Do the float test: drop ½ tsp of masa into a glass of cold water. If it floats, it's ready. If it sinks, beat longer or add a little more lard.
Take a husk, smooth side up, wide end toward you. Spread 2–3 tbsp masa thinly over the top two-thirds, leaving a border at the sides. Add a spoonful of filling.
Fold the sides over each other, then fold the narrow tail up.
Fill the bottom of a tamalera with water below the rack. Stand the tamales upright, open end up. Cover with extra husks and a damp towel, then the lid.
Steam over medium 1¼–1½ hours. They're done when the husk peels away cleanly from the masa. Let rest 15 minutes before serving.

pressureCooker.time: 25 min high pressure + 15 min natural release
steps: Make the filling and masa and assemble the tamales as above. The pork can also go under pressure: 35 minutes high, natural release 10.
Put the trivet in the pot with 1½ cups water. Stand the tamales upright, open end up, snug but not tight. A 6-qt pot holds 12–15.
High pressure 25 minutes, natural release 15.
Let rest 10 minutes. They firm up as they cool.
pressureCooker.note: Reheat frozen tamales at high pressure 15 minutes with 1 cup water.

tips: Drop a coin in the water under the rack. While it rattles there's water; when it goes quiet, add more hot water.

Abuelas say tamales se sienten: make them while angry and they won't cook through, and lift the lid too often and they come out pintos (half raw). A pregnant helper ties a red ribbon around her belly, and some cooks sing to the pot.
The old way to leaven: instead of baking powder, boil tomatillo husks with a pinch of tequesquite, strain, and beat that water into the masa.
Fresh lard from the carnicería makes the masa taste right. The white blocks from the supermarket shelf don't.

variations.name: Tamales de Rajas con Queso
variations.note: The meatless favorite, for Lent or for anyone.

items: Masa from the base, made without the chile and with chicken or vegetable broth
4 poblanos, roasted, peeled and cut in strips
12 oz queso Oaxaca or panela, in sticks

steps: Spread masa on each husk.
Add a few poblano strips, a stick of cheese and a spoonful of salsa verde.
Fold and steam as in the base.
variations.pressureNote: Same as the base: high pressure 25 minutes, natural release 15.

variations.name: Tamales de Dulce
variations.note: Sweet tamales for Christmas and Día de la Candelaria, served with champurrado. On February 2, whoever found the muñeco in the Rosca de Reyes on January 6 pays for the tamales.

items: 1 tsp baking powder and ½ tsp salt
A few drops of red food coloring (the traditional pink) or a little beet juice

steps: Beat the lard until fluffy. Beat in the masa, sugar, baking powder, salt, cinnamon and color until a little ball floats in water.
Fold in the raisins.
Spread on husks with no filling, fold, and steam 1 hour.

recipes.verso: Pásala por el chile y dórala al momento: así se hace el sustento.
recipes.name: Enchiladas Rojas
recipes.en: Red chile enchiladas with queso fresco
recipes.story: Tortillas dipped in red chile, fried and rolled around cheese and onion. In Guanajuato they come topped with fried potatoes and carrots: enchiladas mineras, said to be what miners' wives carried up to the mines. In Real del Monte, Hidalgo, the mineras are made with salsa verde.

ingredients.title: Las enchiladas
items: 2 cups crumbled queso fresco (or queso ranchero)

ingredients.title: Encima
items: 2 potatoes and 2 carrots, diced and boiled
A piece of fried chicken, optional

steps: Toast and soak the chiles. Blend with the garlic, onion, oregano, cumin and 2 cups liquid. Strain.
Fry the sauce in the lard 5 minutes and season. It should be about as thick as cream. Keep warm.
Mix the queso and onion for the filling, saving some for the top.
Heat ½ inch of oil in a skillet. Pass each tortilla through the warm sauce, then fry it 10 seconds per side. (For less splatter, fry first and then dip.)
Fill with cheese and onion, roll, and set on a plate.
Fry the boiled potatoes and carrots in the same oil until golden.
Top with more sauce, the potatoes and carrots, lettuce, chiles en vinagre, crema and the rest of the cheese.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Enchiladas are made at the skillet, one tortilla at a time.
tips: Work fast and serve right away. Enchiladas don't like to wait.

variations.name: Enfrijoladas
variations.note: Tortillas bathed in a seasoned black bean sauce instead of chile.

items: 3 cups frijoles negros de la olla with their broth
Queso fresco, crema and onion; shredded chicken optional

steps: Blend the beans with their broth, the chile and the avocado leaves until smooth, like thin cream.
Simmer 5 minutes and season.
Fry the tortillas lightly, dip them in the bean sauce, and fold in quarters or fill with cheese or chicken.
Top with crema, queso and onion.

recipes.verso: Donde come uno, comen dos.
recipes.name: Frijoles de la Olla
recipes.story: The pot that's always on abuela's stove. Pintos and bayos in the north; bayos, flor de mayo and peruanos as much as black in the center; black beans in the south and along the Gulf. All of them cooked slowly with onion, lard and epazote. The broth matters as much as the beans.

ingredients.title: Frijoles
items: 1 lb dried pinto or black beans

steps: Spread the beans on a tray and pick out stones and broken beans. Rinse well.
Put the beans, water, onion, garlic and lard in a heavy pot (a lead-free clay olla if you have one). Bring to a boil.
Lower to a gentle simmer, partly covered, for 1½–2 hours. If you need more water, add hot water only. Cold water toughens the skins.
When the beans are soft, add the salt and epazote. Simmer 30 minutes more so the salt gets in.
Serve in bowls with their broth, chopped onion, cilantro, serrano and queso fresco, or use them for refritos.

pressureCooker.time: 45 min high pressure + full natural release
steps: Rinse and pick over the beans. No soaking needed.
Put the beans, 8 cups water, onion, garlic and lard in the pot.
High pressure 45 minutes for pintos, 35 for black beans (10–12 if soaked overnight). Let the pressure release naturally, about 25 minutes.
Add the salt and epazote and simmer on Sauté 10–15 minutes.
pressureCooker.note: Don't fill past the halfway line with beans and water. Beans foam.

tips: Salt goes in after the beans are soft.
Clay ollas give the best beans, but buy ones marked Sin Plomo (lead-free). Old or unmarked glazes can leach lead.
Old beans take forever. Buy them where a lot of people buy beans.

variations.name: Frijoles Refritos
variations.note: Fried once, in plenty of lard. Refritos means well-fried, not fried twice.

items: 4 cups cooked beans plus 1 cup of their broth
3–4 tbsp lard (or bacon or chorizo fat)

steps: Heat the lard in a wide skillet and fry the onion until golden. Take the onion out if you like.
Add the beans and broth and mash with a bean masher as they cook.
Keep cooking and stirring about 10 minutes, until thick enough to hold a line when you drag a spoon through. Add broth if it gets too thick.
Top with cheese.

variations.name: Frijoles Charros
variations.note: For carne asada Sundays. In Monterrey, chicharrón goes in at the end. Add a beer and some call them frijoles borrachos; families argue about where one ends and the other begins.

items: 6 cups pinto beans de la olla with their broth
2 hot dogs (salchichas) and 2 slices ham, chopped
½ onion, 2 tomatoes and 2 jalapeños, chopped

steps: Fry the bacon until crisp. Add the chorizo, then the salchicha and ham, and brown.
Add the onion, tomato and jalapeño and cook 5 minutes.
Add the beans with their broth (and the beer). Simmer 20 minutes.
Stir in the cilantro and the chicharrón right before serving.
variations.pressureNote: Cook the beans under pressure as in the base, then finish on Sauté.

recipes.verso: Al arroz, ni lo mires: tápalo y déjalo.
recipes.name: Arroz Rojo
recipes.story: Fried until golden before any liquid goes in, then cooked in tomato broth and left alone. It goes next to everything, and into caldo.

ingredients.title: Arroz
items: 1 carrot, diced, and ½ cup peas, optional

steps: Soak the rice in hot water 10 minutes. Rinse until the water runs clear, then drain very well.
Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium. Add the rice and stir until it turns opaque and light golden and sounds like sand, about 8 minutes.
Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic with ½ cup of the broth. Strain onto the rice and stir 2–3 minutes, until absorbed and the color deepens.
Add the rest of the broth, the salt, carrot, peas, cilantro and serrano. Bring to a boil.
Cover, turn the heat to its lowest setting and cook 18 minutes. Don't lift the lid or stir.
Turn off the heat and let rest 10 minutes, covered. Fluff with a fork.

pressureCooker.time: 4 min high pressure + 10 min natural release
steps: Soak, rinse and drain the rice. Fry it in the oil on Sauté until golden.
Add the strained tomato purée and stir 2 minutes.
Add broth so the total liquid (purée plus broth) is 1¾ cups, then the salt, vegetables, cilantro and serrano. Scrape the bottom well so it won't set off the burn warning.
High pressure 4 minutes, natural release 10. Fluff.

tips: Plenty of abuelas swap some of the salt for a spoon of Knorr caldo de tomate. Nobody has to know.
Lifting the lid lets out the steam, and you get rice that's raw on top and mushy underneath.

variations.name: Arroz Verde
variations.note: The same method with a green purée instead of tomato.

items: The same rice, broth and method as the base

steps: Fry the rice as in the base.
Add the green purée instead of the tomato and cook 2 minutes.
Continue with the broth as in the base.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure time as the base.

recipes.verso: Sin salsa no hay taco, y sin molcajete no hay salsa.
recipes.name: Salsa Roja de Molcajete
recipes.story: Charred on the comal and ground in the volcanic-stone molcajete. Chunky, smoky, and on the table at every meal.

ingredients.title: Salsa
items: ¼ white onion, in one piece

steps: Heat a dry comal or cast-iron pan over medium-high. Char the tomatoes, chiles, garlic and onion, turning, until blistered and soft: about 8 minutes for the garlic and chiles, 12–15 for the tomatoes.
Peel the garlic and grind it with salt in the molcajete into a paste. (If you used chiles de árbol, toast them only a few seconds; they burn fast.)
Add the chiles and grind them. Add the tomatoes one at a time and crush, then the onion.
Thin with a little water and keep it chunky. Taste for salt.
No molcajete? Pulse a few times in a blender. Don't purée.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Salsas come off the comal in minutes.
tips: Season a new molcajete by grinding a handful of raw rice in it, again and again, until the rice comes out white instead of gray.

variations.name: Salsa Verde Cocida
variations.note: The everyday green salsa for tacos, carnitas and chilaquiles.
steps: Simmer the tomatillos and chiles 8 minutes, until olive green.
Blend with the garlic, onion, cilantro, salt and a few spoons of the cooking water.

variations.name: Salsa de Chile de Árbol
variations.note: The thin, fiery red salsa from the taquería.
steps: Toast the chiles in a dry pan 30 seconds, stirring, until fragrant. Don't let them blacken.
Simmer the tomatillos 8 minutes.
Blend everything until smooth. Strain if you want it silky.

recipes.verso: Café de olla y pan dulce: la tarde no pide más.
recipes.name: Café de Olla
recipes.en: Clay-pot coffee with piloncillo and cinnamon
recipes.story: Coffee brewed in a clay olla with piloncillo and canela. Popular history credits the Adelitas of the Revolution with brewing it for the troops. Coffee only reached Mexico in the 1700s, so it isn't pre-Hispanic, but it is what abuela still pours with pan dulce.

ingredients.title: Café
items: 3 oz piloncillo, chopped or grated (or ⅓ cup dark brown sugar)
½ cup coarsely ground dark-roast coffee (Mexican, from Veracruz, Chiapas or Oaxaca, if you can)

steps: Put the water, piloncillo, cinnamon and any spices in a clay olla or a saucepan. Bring to a boil and cook until the piloncillo dissolves, about 5 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the coffee, cover and let it steep 5 minutes.
Strain through a fine strainer or a cloth.
Serve hot in clay jarritos or mugs, with pan dulce.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. It's a 15-minute steep.
tips: Don't let the coffee keep boiling. Add it off the heat, or let it rise to a boil once and turn it off; boiled coffee turns bitter.
Buy ollas and jarritos marked Sin Plomo (lead-free). Profeco's test: soak part of the piece in white vinegar for 24 hours; if the glaze turns dull or rough, don't cook in it.
A clay olla gives the coffee its earthy taste. Season a new one by boiling water in it a few times before the first coffee.
Use a coarse grind, like for a French press, so it strains clean.

variations.name: Chocolate Caliente
variations.note: Made with water in Oaxaca, with milk most other places. Frothed with a molinillo until foamy.
steps: Heat the milk (or water) with the cinnamon and salt until steaming. Don't let it boil over.
Add the chocolate and whisk until melted.
Take out the cinnamon and froth with a molinillo, rolling it between your palms, or a whisk, until the top is foamy.
Serve right away with pan dulce.

variations.name: Café con Leche
variations.note: Half café, half hot milk, for dunking conchas.
steps: Heat the milk until steaming.
Pour half coffee, half milk into each cup and sweeten to taste.

recipes.verso: Champurrado y tamal, ¡ni el frío nos hace mal!
recipes.name: Champurrado
recipes.story: A thick chocolate atole made with masa, sweetened with piloncillo and frothed with a wooden molinillo. It's for cold mornings, posadas and Día de Muertos, with tamales.

ingredients.title: Champurrado
items: ½ cup masa harina (or 4 oz fresh masa)
4 cups water (the traditional way), milk, or half and half
1 tablet (3 oz) Mexican chocolate, chopped (chocolate de metate if you can find it)
3–4 oz piloncillo, grated (or ⅓ cup brown sugar)

steps: Whisk the masa into the warm water until there are no lumps. Strain.
In a pot, simmer the water or milk with the cinnamon, piloncillo, salt and anise for 10 minutes.
Add the chocolate and whisk until melted.
Pour in the masa mixture slowly, whisking constantly.
Simmer on low, stirring constantly, 10 minutes until thick enough to coat a spoon. Take out the cinnamon.
Froth with a molinillo, rolling it between your palms, or with a whisk. Serve hot.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Atole needs constant stirring, and masa scorches under pressure.
tips: Keep stirring. Masa sticks to the bottom and burns fast.

variations.name: Atole Blanco con Canela
variations.note: The plain atole underneath every flavored one.
steps: Dissolve the masa in 2 cups of the liquid and strain.
Simmer the rest of the liquid with the cinnamon and sugar.
Whisk in the masa and cook, stirring, 10 minutes until thick. Add the vanilla.

recipes.verso: Agua de jamaica, roja y bien fría: la que se toma todo el día.
recipes.name: Agua de Jamaica
recipes.story: Deep red hibiscus water, tart and cold. A jug of agua fresca sits on the table at la comida, the big midday meal.

ingredients.title: Agua
items: ½–¾ cup sugar or grated piloncillo

steps: Rinse the flowers.
Boil 4 cups of the water with the flowers and cinnamon 5 minutes. Turn off the heat and steep 15 minutes.
Strain, pressing on the flowers. Stir in the sugar while it's warm.
Add the remaining 4 cups of cold water. Taste and adjust. Serve over ice.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version needed. It's a quick steep.
tips: The flowers make a second, lighter batch. Or sauté them with onion and garlic for tacos de jamaica.

variations.name: Horchata de Arroz
variations.note: Mexican horchata is made from rice and canela.

items: ½ cup milk or evaporated milk, optional

steps: Soak the rice and cinnamon in 4 cups hot water overnight.
Blend the rice, cinnamon and soaking water 2 minutes until very fine.
Strain through a cloth or a very fine strainer.
Add the remaining water, the sugar, vanilla and milk. Serve over ice, stirring before you pour because it settles.

recipes.verso: A la hora del cafecito, una concha y un ratito.
recipes.name: Conchas
recipes.story: The best-known pan dulce: a soft, slightly sweet bun under a crunchy sugar topping scored like a seashell. Picked up warm from the panadería with tongs and a tray, and eaten with café or chocolate.

ingredients.title: Masa (dough)
items: 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose or bread flour
¾ cup (180 ml) warm whole milk
6 tbsp (85 g) soft butter, plus a little melted butter for brushing

ingredients.title: Cubierta (topping)
items: ⅓ cup (65 g) vegetable shortening (manteca vegetal); butter works but spreads and blurs the shell

steps: Mix the flour, sugar, yeast and salt in a large bowl or stand mixer. Add the milk, eggs and vanilla and mix into a shaggy dough.
Knead 8–10 minutes (or with the dough hook on medium) until smooth. Add the butter a spoon at a time, kneading until each piece disappears. The dough should be soft, a little tacky and stretchy.
Cover and let rise in a warm place 1½–2 hours, until doubled.
Make the topping: mix the flour, powdered sugar, shortening and vanilla into a smooth paste like play dough. Divide into 12 balls.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces (about 85 g each). Roll each into a smooth ball and set on parchment-lined sheet pans, 3 inches apart. Press each down slightly and brush with a little melted butter.
Flatten each topping ball between two pieces of plastic into a 3½-inch disc. Lay it on a bun and press gently so it sticks.
Score the topping in a shell pattern with a concha cutter or a sharp knife: curved lines fanning out from one side. Cut only through the topping, not the dough.
Cover loosely and let rise 1 hour, until puffy. The topping will crack open along the lines.
Bake at 350°F for 18–20 minutes, until the bottoms are golden. The tops should stay pale.
Cool a few minutes and eat warm.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Bread needs the oven.
tips: Brushing the buns with butter before the topping goes on keeps it from sliding off.
Panaderos make the topping 1:1:1 by weight: flour, powdered sugar and shortening. In humid weather, add a spoonful more flour so it doesn't slide.
If your kitchen is cold, let the dough rise in the oven with only the light on.
Conchas go stale fast. Freeze extras the same day and warm them 5 minutes in the oven.

variations.name: Pan de Muerto
variations.note: Made for the ofrenda in late October and early November. An orange-blossom sweet bread decorated with dough bones and a round skull, brushed with butter and rolled in sugar. The four bones in a cross point to the four directions; some say they are tears. In Oaxaca it's pan de yema with a little face on top.

items: Concha dough from the base, with these changes: add the zest of 2 oranges, 1 tbsp orange blossom water (agua de azahar) and, if you like, ½ tsp anise seed, ground; use ½ cup milk plus ¼ cup orange juice instead of ¾ cup milk

steps: Make the dough and let it rise as in the base, steps 1–3.
Set aside about a quarter of the dough. Divide the rest into 2 or 3 pieces and shape each into a smooth round loaf on a lined sheet pan.

With the reserved dough, roll ropes and press your fingers along them to make knobby bones (huesos). Lay 4 across each loaf in a cross, and set a small ball (the skull) in the center. Stick them on with a little beaten egg.
Let rise 1 hour, brush with beaten egg and bake at 350°F for 30–35 minutes, until deep golden.
While warm, brush all over with melted butter and roll or sprinkle with sugar.

variations.name: Conchas de Chocolate
variations.note: Every panadería tray has white and chocolate side by side. Make half and half.

items: Topping from the base, with 2 tbsp of the flour replaced by cocoa powder

steps: Make the topping with cocoa.
Top, score, rise and bake as in the base.

recipes.verso: Pa'l susto, un bolillo.
recipes.name: Bolillos
recipes.story: Mexico's everyday bread: crackly crust, soft inside, pointed at both ends. It's for molletes, tortas, capirotada and dunking in caldo. Abuelas also say a bite of bolillo calms a scare (para el susto). It came out of French baking during the Intervention of the 1860s. In Guadalajara its cousin is the birote salado, slightly sour and firm-crusted: the bread of the torta ahogada.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Add the water and lard and mix into a dough.
Knead 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and let rise 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
Divide into 10 pieces (about 85 g). Flatten each into an oval, then roll it up tightly from a long side into a log, pressing the seam closed.
Roll the ends under your palms so they taper to points. Set seam side down on a lined sheet pan.
Cover and let rise 45 minutes, until puffy.
Heat the oven to 425°F with an empty pan on the bottom rack. Slash each roll once down the length, about ¼ inch deep.
Spray or brush the rolls with water. Put them in the oven and pour a cup of hot water into the empty pan for steam. Close the door fast.
Bake 20–25 minutes, until golden and they sound hollow when you tap the bottom. Cool on a rack.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Bread needs the oven, and steam in the oven is what makes the crust crackle.
tips: The steam is the secret to the thin, crackly crust. Don't skip the pan of water.
Day-old bolillos are perfect for molletes and capirotada.

variations.name: Teleras
variations.note: The soft, flat roll for tortas, with two grooves across the top.
steps: Divide the dough into 8 pieces and shape into flat ovals about ¾ inch thick.
Press two deep lines along the length of each with the handle of a wooden spoon, almost to the bottom.
Rise 45 minutes and bake at 400°F for 18–20 minutes, without steam, so the crust stays soft.

recipes.verso: Arroz con leche, me quiero casar…
recipes.name: Arroz con Leche
recipes.story: Rice cooked first in water with cinnamon and lime peel, then slowly in milk. Every abuela has a strong opinion about raisins. Kids know it from the playground song: «Arroz con leche, me quiero casar con una señorita de San Nicolás…»

ingredients.title: Arroz con leche
items: 1 strip lime peel, no white pith

steps: Rinse the rice and soak 15 minutes. Drain.
Simmer the rice in the water with the cinnamon, lime peel and salt until the water is absorbed, about 15 minutes.
Add the milk and sugar. Simmer on low, stirring often, 25–30 minutes until creamy.
Take out the peel and cinnamon. Stir in the vanilla and raisins and cook 5 minutes more.
It thickens as it cools. Serve warm or cold with ground cinnamon.

pressureCooker.time: 12 min high pressure + 10 min natural release
steps: Put the rice, water, cinnamon, lime peel and salt in the pot.
High pressure 12 minutes, natural release 10.
Switch to Sauté. Add the milk and sugar and stir constantly 8–10 minutes until creamy; it scorches easily.
Finish with the vanilla and raisins.

tips: Use Mexican canela (Ceylon cinnamon), the soft, flaky kind. Cassia sticks are harder and spicier.

variations.name: Arroz con Leche Cremoso
variations.note: The richer version many families make now.

items: The same rice, water and spices as the base
1 can (14 oz) sweetened condensed milk (instead of the sugar)

steps: Cook the rice in the water as in the base.
Add 2 cups milk, the condensed milk and the evaporated milk. Simmer, stirring, 20 minutes.
variations.pressureNote: Same as the base. Add the canned milks on Sauté.

recipes.verso: Tiembla, tiembla, pero no se cae: así es el flan de la abuela.
recipes.name: Flan de la Abuela
recipes.story: The old-style flan: whole milk infused with cinnamon and lime peel, plus eggs and sugar, baked in a water bath under a layer of dark caramel.
steps: Heat the milk with the sugar, cinnamon and lime peel until steaming. Turn off the heat and steep 15 minutes. Remove the cinnamon and peel and let cool until warm.
Make the caramel: cook the sugar and water in a small pan without stirring, swirling the pan, until deep amber. Pour into an 8- or 9-inch flan mold and tilt to coat the bottom.
Whisk the eggs and yolks gently. You don't want bubbles. Slowly whisk in the warm milk and the vanilla. Strain into the mold.
Cover with foil. Set the mold in a larger pan and pour in hot water halfway up the sides (baño maría).
Bake at 350°F 50–60 minutes, until the edges are set and the center jiggles like gelatin.
Cool, then chill at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
Run a knife around the edge, put a plate on top and flip it in one quick move.

pressureCooker.time: 9 min high pressure + 10 min natural release (ramekins)
steps: Make the custard and caramel as above, but divide among 6 heatproof ramekins that fit in your pot. Cover each with foil.
Put the trivet in the pot with 1½ cups water and stack the ramekins on it.
High pressure 9 minutes, natural release 10.
Cool, then chill at least 4 hours before unmolding.
pressureCooker.note: For one mold that fits your pot, time depends on its size and depth. In a stovetop olla exprés, Mexican cooks count about 10–15 minutes from the whistle for the classic and about 25 for napolitano. In an electric pot, start at 15–20 minutes for the classic and 25 for napolitano, then check: the center should jiggle, not slosh.

tips: Strain the custard. That's what makes a flan smooth, with no holes.
Low and slow. An oven that's too hot gives a spongy flan full of bubbles.

variations.name: Flan Napolitano
variations.note: The popular modern flan: richer, denser and blended in a minute. Most families make this one now, and they argue about whether it needs queso crema.
steps: Blend everything 1 minute.
Pour over the caramel, cover, and bake in a water bath at 350°F 50–60 minutes.
Chill overnight and unmold.
variations.pressureNote: Same as the base: ramekins at high pressure 9 minutes, natural release 10.

recipes.verso: Capirotada en Cuaresma: cada capa, una promesa.
recipes.name: Capirotada
recipes.story: The bread pudding of Cuaresma (Lent): layers of fried bolillo, raisins, nuts and cheese soaked in spiced piloncillo syrup. Old recipes from Jalisco and Colima simmer a tomato and an onion in the syrup. It sounds strange and tastes right. Every layer means something: the bread is the body of Christ, the syrup his blood, the canela the wood of the cross, the cloves the nails, and the white cheese the holy shroud. It's eaten on the Fridays of Lent and on Viernes Santo.

ingredients.title: La miel
items: 1 Roma tomato and ¼ onion, optional, the old way

ingredients.title: Las capas
items: 6 day-old bolillos, sliced ½ inch thick
½ cup peanuts or slivered almonds
2 cups shredded queso añejo, cotija or Chihuahua

steps: Simmer the piloncillo, water, cinnamon and cloves (and the tomato and onion) 15 minutes, until syrupy. Strain.
Fry the bread slices in butter until golden on both sides, or brush them with butter and toast in the oven.
Butter a baking dish. Layer bread, raisins, nuts and cheese, and repeat for 3 layers.
Pour the syrup slowly over everything so it all soaks in.
Cover with foil and bake at 350°F for 30 minutes. Uncover and bake 10 minutes more.
Let rest 15 minutes and top with sprinkles. Serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Capirotada needs the dry heat of the oven to set.
tips: Toast the bread well. Pale bread turns to mush.

chiles.name: Pasilla
chiles.uses: Mole poblano, mole de olla, salsa borracha

chiles.name: Piquín · Chiltepín
chiles.uses: Crushed over menudo and pozole, on fruit

glossary.definition: Dough of nixtamalized corn. Fresh masa from a tortillería is best. For tamales ask for masa para tamal, sin preparar (unprepared), ground coarser than tortilla masa. Masa harina is the dried flour version.
Rendered pork lard. Buy it fresh and soft from a carnicería. The shelf-stable white blocks are hydrogenated and taste flat.
A different plant from Mediterranean oregano, more citrusy and grassy. Rub it between your palms over the pot or bowl.
Mexican (Ceylon) cinnamon: soft, flaky layered bark that breaks in your fingers. Milder and sweeter than cassia.
A pungent herb for black beans, quesadillas, chilaquiles and pozole verde. There's no real substitute; leave it out if you can't find it.
A big heart-shaped leaf that tastes of anise and sassafras. Used in pozole verde, pipián and Oaxacan moles.
Dried Mexican avocado leaves, toasted before using. They add an anise note to barbacoa and black beans.
Unrefined cane sugar pressed into cones. Grate it or melt it in water. Dark brown sugar is the closest swap.
Annatto seeds ground with spices into recado rojo paste. Sold in bricks; the base of cochinita pibil.
Seville sour orange, used in the Yucatán. Swap: two parts orange juice to one part lime juice.
The large white corn for pozole. Bagged precooked maíz pozolero beats canned hominy.
A sour cactus fruit for mole de olla and salsas. Lime juice can stand in.
Queso fresco crumbles; cotija and añejo are dry and salty; Oaxaca and asadero melt and stretch; panela holds its shape when warm.
Mexican cultured cream, thinner and saltier than sour cream. Thin sour cream with a little milk if you can't find it.
Glazed clay ollas, cazuelas and jarritos for beans, coffee and atole. Buy pieces marked Sin Plomo (lead-free); old or unmarked glazes can leach lead.
A natural mineral salt from the old lakebeds of central Mexico, the traditional leavening for tamales, dissolved in water (often with tomatillo husks).
